title: [YouPass Collect] - Global oil consumption trends 2009-2030
prompt: The graph below shows information about the total oil consumption of four major consumers from 2009 to 2030. Summarize the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

frame.name: Introduction
paragraphs: The line graph illustrates the amount of oil consumed daily by four major regions, namely the USA, China, the Middle East, and Western Europe and Japan, over a 21-year period from 2009 to 2030.

frame.name: Overview
paragraphs: Overall, the data reveals mixed consumption patterns, with only the Middle East experiencing sustained growth throughout the period, while Western Europe and Japan recorded a consistent decline. Meanwhile, both the USA and China are projected to increase to a peak before falling by 2030. Additionally, the USA remains the largest consumer throughout, though its lead diminishes considerably over time.

frame.name: Body 1
paragraphs: Looking at the two regions starting at the same baseline, both China and the Middle East began at 2 million barrels per day in 2009. The Middle East witnessed a steady upward trend throughout the period, rising to 2.3 million barrels in 2015, continuing to 2.5 million in 2025, and reaching 3 million barrels by 2030. China also experienced growth, increasing to 2.8 million barrels in 2015, then surging more sharply to a peak of 3.9 million barrels in 2025, before declining slightly to 3.5 million barrels at the end of the period.

frame.name: Body 2
paragraphs: Regarding the two regions with higher initial consumption, the USA started at 9 million barrels per day in 2009, more than double that of Western Europe and Japan at 4 million barrels. Western Europe and Japan saw a continuous decline throughout the entire period, falling from 4 million barrels to 3 million in 2015, further decreasing to 2.4 million in 2025, and ending at the lowest figure of 1.9 million barrels in 2030. Meanwhile, the USA followed a more complex pattern, initially rising to a peak of 10 million barrels in 2015, before gradually declining to 8 million barrels in 2025 and finishing at 7.8 million barrels in the final year.
